memories.content: Complete the problem framing within the first two sentences so the reader reaches the proposal's central issue before any supporting background.
Use the first sentence for the concrete problem and the second for its consequence; reserve later sentences for the proposed response.
Specify the user, context, and interaction to be explored in the primary HCI research question.
Provide one compact visual summary when proposing an unfamiliar interaction procedure.
Mark the conditions that move an unfamiliar interaction procedure from one step to the next in its visual summary.
Present the master’s research schedule as phased periods for exploration, design, prototyping, and user evaluation.
Link one reviewable deliverable to each phase of the master’s research.
Place the gap left by HCI-related research and the proposed design and empirical contributions in close proximity.
Divide a two-page proposal with short descriptive subheadings so a reader can jump directly to the problem, proposed response, and next steps.
Give the problem and proposed response their own descriptive subheadings instead of relying only on paragraph transitions.
Give the next steps and requested support their own descriptive subheading so they remain easy to find on a return visit.
Place pilot observation or initial prototype results near sentences supporting feasibility claims.
Readers often decide what a proposal is about from its first two sentences before scanning the rest of the page.
When setup continues past the second sentence, readers who are skimming often retain the background topic but miss the exact problem being proposed.
Reuse the same short subheadings in discussion so a reader can return to a section without searching through the whole page.
Use visible subheadings as a completeness check: an empty or missing section makes an omitted part of the proposal immediately apparent.
Readers often scan section labels before deciding which paragraph to read closely.
Do not change names referring to the same user roles, system functions, or operational stages midway.
Use abbreviations only for long recurring terms in a two-page proposal.
Present the full term and abbreviation together when using an abbreviation for the first time.
Refer to participants based on the roles they perform in the study rather than their status.
Reviewers from different subfields find it difficult to infer an abbreviation from context alone when it is not defined at first use.
When introducing an operational role for the first time, define both the decisions it can make and the actions it performs.
Individuals holding identical job titles may possess different system modification privileges and data access rights depending on their deployment site.
The user tends to group distinct field roles under the single label “user.”

analysis.overview: The frames address complementary but nonoverlapping aspects of proposal quality. The reference frame emphasizes structure, early problem framing, research design, visual explanation, scheduling, evidence placement, and navigation; the compared frame focuses on stable terminology, abbreviations, and precise role definitions.

relations.reason: The memories jointly give an opening structure and explain that readers use those sentences to identify the proposal, while extended setup can obscure the exact problem.
relations.summary: State the concrete problem and its consequence within the first two sentences, leaving the proposed response for later.

relations.reason: The memories jointly identify role-based naming as the corrective to collapsing distinct field roles under the label “user.”

relations.reason: The memories jointly require capability-based role definitions and explain why job titles alone may not determine operational authority across deployments.
relations.summary: Define an operational role by its decisions and actions, accounting for site-dependent modification privileges and data access.

reports.compared_only: Compared-only guidance covers consistent naming, restrained and defined abbreviations, role-based participant labels, and operational-role definitions grounded in permissions, actions, and site variation.
reports.reference_only: Reference-only guidance covers opening clarity, research-question specificity, procedure visuals, phased schedules, gap-to-contribution linkage, descriptive navigation, completeness checks, and evidence near feasibility claims.
